title: What Is MCP?
description: Understand the Model Context Protocol — the open standard that connects AI models to tools, databases, and services.

data.text: MCP — the Model Context Protocol — is an open standard introduced by Anthropic in 2024 that is quickly becoming the universal language for connecting AI models to external tools and data sources.

Before MCP, making an AI model interact with an external system — your file system, a database, a code editor, a calendar — required custom one-off engineering for every combination of model and tool. The integrations were brittle, non-transferable, and expensive to maintain. MCP solves this by defining a single, open standard that any AI model and any tool can implement once and immediately interoperate. It is, in practical terms, the plumbing layer that makes AI agents genuinely useful in real workflows.
Why MCP was created

Before MCP, every AI tool had its own custom integration with every service. If you wanted your AI to access your database, your calendar, and your code editor, each required a custom one-off implementation. MCP creates a standard API that works once and works everywhere.

data.title: The USB analogy
data.text: Before USB, every device needed a different, incompatible cable. USB created one standard plug that works everywhere. MCP does the same for AI tools → external tools.

The problem MCP solves is sometimes called the M×N integration problem. If you have M different AI models and N different tools, and each requires a custom integration, you end up with M×N separate implementations to build and maintain. MCP collapses this to M+N: each AI implements the MCP client once, each tool implements the MCP server once, and they all interoperate automatically. The larger the ecosystem grows, the more valuable the standard becomes.

data.text: How MCP works

MCP defines a client-server architecture. The AI application (Claude Desktop, Cursor, a custom app) acts as the MCP client. External capabilities are exposed as MCP servers — lightweight programs that run locally or remotely and advertise a set of tools, resources, and prompts that the AI can use. The AI model queries the MCP server to discover what is available, then calls specific tools when needed during a conversation or task.

data.text: MCP servers expose three types of primitives: tools (functions the AI can call, like read_file or create_issue), resources (data sources the AI can read, like a file or a database row), and prompts (pre-defined interaction templates). Most users only encounter tools — they are the most common and the most powerful primitive. Resources and prompts are more relevant for developers building custom MCP servers.

rows: A function the AI can call to take an action or retrieve data
A data source the AI can read as context
A local file, a database table, a webpage
A pre-built interaction template for common workflows
A template for code review, bug triage, or document summarisation

data.text: Local vs. remote MCP servers

MCP servers can run in two places. Local MCP servers run as processes on your own machine — the filesystem MCP server, for example, runs locally so the AI can read and write files on your computer without sending them to an external service. Remote MCP servers run as cloud services — a Slack MCP server or a GitHub MCP server runs on a server and the AI connects to it over HTTPS. Both follow the same MCP protocol; the difference is where the server process lives and who controls it.

data.text: MCP in practice: what it looks like to use it

data.title: Example: Claude Desktop with filesystem and GitHub MCP
data.content:
A developer configures Claude Desktop with two MCP servers: the official filesystem server (pointing to their project directory) and the GitHub MCP server (authenticated to their account).

They can now ask Claude:
- "Read the README in my project folder and suggest improvements" → filesystem MCP reads the file
- "What open issues are assigned to me in the repo?" → GitHub MCP queries the API
- "Create a draft PR description based on the changes in this branch" → GitHub MCP fetches the diff; filesystem MCP reads relevant files

All of this happens in a single conversation. Claude orchestrates the tool calls, assembles the context, and generates a coherent response. No copy-pasting between apps required.

data.title: Example: AI coding agent with MCP
data.content:
A developer using Cursor (an AI code editor with MCP support) connects it to a Postgres MCP server pointing at their development database.

They ask: "Why is the users table missing indexes on the email column? Write a migration to fix it."

Cursor's AI:
1. Calls the Postgres MCP server to inspect the users table schema
2. Confirms the missing index
3. Generates a SQL migration file
4. Uses the filesystem MCP to write the migration to the correct directory

The entire workflow — schema inspection, diagnosis, fix generation, file creation — happens without the developer switching context or manually querying the database.

data.text: MCP and security: what to know
MCP gives AI models real access to real systems. That power comes with real risk if not configured carefully. A few principles worth keeping in mind when setting up MCP servers.

Scope your MCP servers narrowly. A filesystem MCP server pointed at your home directory gives the AI access to everything on your machine. Pointed at a specific project folder, it can only see what is relevant. Always configure the narrowest scope that covers your use case.

Prefer read-only access where possible. Many MCP servers support read-only modes. If your use case is reviewing and summarising — not creating or modifying — configure the server accordingly. A read-only GitHub MCP cannot accidentally create issues or close pull requests.

Be cautious with remote MCP servers from unknown sources. Local MCP servers run on your machine and you control them. A remote MCP server is a service you are connecting your AI to — verify it is from a trusted source before granting it access to your data or accounts.

data.title: Do I need to understand MCP deeply?
data.text: Not right now. What matters: MCP is why AI tools can increasingly connect to everything else you use. As more tools adopt it, AI agents will become dramatically more useful for everyday workflows.
MCP for non-developers: what changes for you

You do not need to build or configure MCP servers to benefit from them. As MCP adoption spreads, AI applications will increasingly come with pre-configured integrations that just work — similar to how apps today connect to Google or Microsoft accounts with one click. The experience for an end user will be: open the AI app, connect your tools via a simple auth flow, and start asking the AI to work across them.

What MCP means for everyday users in the near term: AI assistants that can genuinely work across your tools rather than being isolated to a single chat window. An AI that can read your project files, check your calendar, look up relevant emails, and draft a status update — without you having to copy-paste context from each source — is a qualitatively different kind of tool. MCP is the infrastructure layer that makes that possible.
